questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave pulse travelling on a string at a speed of $40 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ in the negative $x$-direction has its maximum located at $x = 0$ when $t = 0$. Where will this maximum be found at $t = 5 \text{ s}$?
questions.solution:
Given speed of the wave pulse, $v = 40 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 0.4 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Since the wave is travelling in the negative $x$-direction, the position of the maximum at time $t$ is given by $x = -vt$.

Substituting the values for $t = 5 \text{ s}$:

$x = - (0.4 \text{ m s}^{-1}) \times 5 \text{ s} = -2 \text{ m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave travelling on a string stretched along the $X$-axis has an equation given by $y = A\, e^{-\left(\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T}\right)^2}$. Identify the direction in which the wave is travelling.
questions.solution:
The given equation of the wave is $y = A e^{-\left(\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T}\right)^2}$.

For a point on the wave with a constant phase, we have:

$\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T} = \text{constant}$

Differentiating with respect to time $t$, we get:

$\dfrac{1}{a} \dfrac{dx}{dt} + \dfrac{1}{T} = 0$

$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\dfrac{a}{T}$

Since the wave velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ is negative, the wave is travelling in the negative $x$-direction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave travelling on a string stretched along the $X$-axis has an equation given by $y = A\, e^{-\left(\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T}\right)^2}$. Locate the maximum of the pulse at $t = T$ and at $t = 2T$ respectively.
questions.solution:
The given equation of the wave is $y = A e^{-\left(\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T}\right)^2}$.

The maximum value of the pulse occurs when the exponent is zero, since the function $e^{-z^2}$ is maximum at $z = 0$.

$\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T} = 0$

$x = -\dfrac{a}{T} t$

At $t = T$, the position of the maximum is:

$x = -\dfrac{a}{T} (T) = -a$

At $t = 2T$, the position of the maximum is:

$x = -\dfrac{a}{T} (2T) = -2a$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave travelling on a string stretched along the $X$-axis has an equation given by $y = A\, e^{-\left(\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T}\right)^2}$. Determine the dimensions of $A$, $a$, and $T$.
questions.solution:
The argument of the exponential function must be dimensionless. Therefore, the terms $\dfrac{x}{a}$ and $\dfrac{t}{T}$ are dimensionless.

Since $x$ represents position, its dimension is $L$. For $\dfrac{x}{a}$ to be dimensionless, the dimension of $a$ must be $L$.

Since $t$ represents time, its dimension is $T$. For $\dfrac{t}{T}$ to be dimensionless, the dimension of $T$ must be $T$.

The exponential term $e^{-\left(\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T}\right)^2}$ is a dimensionless quantity. Therefore, the dimension of $A$ must be the same as the dimension of $y$.

Since $y$ represents the displacement of the wave, its dimension is $L$. Thus, the dimension of $A$ is $L$.

The dimensions of $A$, $a$, and $T$ are $L$, $L$, and $T$ respectively.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave travelling on a string stretched along the $X$-axis has an equation given by $y = A\, e^{-\left(\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T}\right)^2}$. Compute the wave speed.
questions.solution:
The equation of the given wave is $y = A e^{-\left(\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T}\right)^2}$

For a travelling wave, the phase is constant for a given point on the waveform:

$\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{t}{T} = \text{constant}$

Differentiating with respect to time $t$:

$\dfrac{1}{a}\dfrac{dx}{dt} + \dfrac{1}{T} = 0$

$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\dfrac{a}{T}$

The wave speed is the magnitude of the wave velocity:

$v = \left|\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right| = \dfrac{a}{T}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A stretched string carries a wave in the positive $x$-direction with a wave speed of $v$. The displacement of the particle at $x = 0$ is described by $f(t) = A \sin(t/T)$. Determine the wave equation.
questions.solution:
For a wave traveling in the positive $x$-direction with speed $v$, the displacement $f(x, t)$ at any position $x$ and time $t$ is given by the displacement at $x = 0$ at an earlier time $t - \dfrac{x}{v}$.

Given the displacement at $x = 0$ is $f(t) = A \sin\left(\dfrac{t}{T}\right)$.

Substituting $t$ with $t - \dfrac{x}{v}$ gives the wave equation:

$f(x, t) = A \sin\left(\dfrac{t - \dfrac{x}{v}}{T}\right)$

$f(x, t) = A \sin\left(\dfrac{t}{T} - \dfrac{x}{vT}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A pulse travelling on a string is described by the function $y = \dfrac{a^3}{(x - vt)^2 + a^2}$, where $a = 5 \text{ mm}$ and $v = 20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. Taking $x = 0$ at the middle of the string, determine the positions of the peak of the pulse at $t = 0$, $1 \text{ s}$, and $2 \text{ s}$ respectively.
questions.solution:
The equation of the pulse is $y = \dfrac{a^3}{(x - vt)^2 + a^2}$.

The peak of the pulse occurs where the displacement $y$ is maximum. This happens when the denominator is minimum, which corresponds to $(x - vt)^2 = 0$.

Thus, the position of the peak at any time $t$ is given by $x = vt$.

Given the velocity of the pulse $v = 20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

At $t = 0$, the position of the peak is $x = 20 \times 0 = 0$.

At $t = 1 \text{ s}$, the position of the peak is $x = 20 \times 1 = 20 \text{ cm}$.

At $t = 2 \text{ s}$, the position of the peak is $x = 20 \times 2 = 40 \text{ cm}$.

questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: The figure displays a wave pulse at $t = 0$. The pulse travels to the right with a speed of $10 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. Determine the respective rightward shifts of the shape of the string at $t = 1 \text{ s}$, $2 \text{ s}$ and $3 \text{ s}$.
questions.solution:
The speed of the wave pulse is given as $v = 10 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

The rightward shift of the wave pulse in time $t$ is the distance traveled by it, which is given by $d = v \times t$.

At $t = 1 \text{ s}$, the shift is $d_1 = 10 \text{ cm s}^{-1} \times 1 \text{ s} = 10 \text{ cm}$.

At $t = 2 \text{ s}$, the shift is $d_2 = 10 \text{ cm s}^{-1} \times 2 \text{ s} = 20 \text{ cm}$.

At $t = 3 \text{ s}$, the shift is $d_3 = 10 \text{ cm s}^{-1} \times 3 \text{ s} = 30 \text{ cm}$.

Therefore, the respective rightward shifts are $10 \text{ cm}$, $20 \text{ cm}$, and $30 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave pulse travels on a string towards the positive $X$-axis with a speed $v$. At $t = 0$, the shape of the string is given by $g(x) = A \sin(x/a)$, where $A$ and $a$ are constants. Write the equation of the wave for a general time $t$.
questions.solution:
For a wave traveling in the positive $x$-direction with speed $v$, the wave equation $f(x, t)$ must be a function of $(x - vt)$.

Given the shape of the wave at $t = 0$ is $g(x) = A \sin\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)$.

Replacing $x$ with $(x - vt)$ in the expression for $g(x)$ gives the equation of the wave at any general time $t$.

Thus, $f(x, t) = g(x - vt) = A \sin\left(\dfrac{x - vt}{a}\right)$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave pulse travels on a string towards the positive $X$-axis with a speed $v$. At $t = 0$, the shape of the string is given by $g(x) = A \sin(x/a)$, where $A$ and $a$ are constants. Determine the dimensions of $A$ and $a$.
questions.solution:
The displacement of the string $g(x)$ has the dimension of length, so $[g(x)] = [L]$.

From the given equation $g(x) = A \sin(x/a)$, the amplitude $A$ must have the same dimension as $g(x)$.

Therefore, $[A] = [L]$.

The argument of the trigonometric function must be dimensionless. Thus, $[x/a] = [M^0 L^0 T^0]$.

Since $x$ represents position, $[x] = [L]$.

Therefore, $[a] = [x] = [L]$.

The dimensions of $A$ and $a$ are $L$ and $L$ respectively.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave travels on a string in the positive $x$-direction at a velocity $v$. The shape of the string at $t = t_0$ is described by $g(x, t_0) = A \sin(x/a)$. Determine the wave equation for a general time $t$.
questions.solution:
The general equation of a wave traveling in the positive $x$-direction with velocity $v$ is given by $f(x, t) = h(x - vt)$.

At $t = t_0$, the wave equation is given as $f(x, t_0) = h(x - vt_0) = A \sin\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)$.

Let $z = x - vt_0$, which implies $x = z + vt_0$.

Substituting this into the function gives $h(z) = A \sin\left(\dfrac{z + vt_0}{a}\right)$.

For a general time $t$, replace $z$ with $x - vt$:

$f(x, t) = h(x - vt) = A \sin\left(\dfrac{x - vt + vt_0}{a}\right)$

$f(x, t) = A \sin\left(\dfrac{x - v(t - t_0)}{a}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave travelling on a string has the equation $y = (0.10 \text{ mm}) \sin[(31.4 \text{ m}^{-1})x + (314 \text{ s}^{-1})t]$. In which direction does the wave travel?
questions.solution:
The given equation of the wave is $y = (0.10 \text{ mm}) \sin[(31.4 \text{ m}^{-1})x + (314 \text{ s}^{-1})t]$.

Comparing this with the standard wave equation $y = A \sin(kx + \omega t)$, we observe that the argument of the sine function has a positive sign between the spatial and temporal terms.

For a point of constant phase, $kx + \omega t = \text{constant}$.

Differentiating with respect to time $t$, we get $k \dfrac{dx}{dt} + \omega = 0$, which gives the wave velocity $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -\dfrac{\omega}{k}$.

Since the velocity is negative, the wave travels in the negative $x$-direction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave travelling on a string has the equation $y = (0.10 \text{ mm}) \sin[(31.4 \text{ m}^{-1})x + (314 \text{ s}^{-1})t]$. Determine the wave speed, the wavelength and the frequency of the wave.
questions.solution:
Comparing the given wave equation $y = (0.10 \text{ mm}) \sin[(31.4 \text{ m}^{-1})x + (314 \text{ s}^{-1})t]$ with the standard wave equation $y = A \sin(kx + \omega t)$, we get:

$k = 31.4 \text{ m}^{-1}$ and $\omega = 314 \text{ s}^{-1}$

The wave speed is given by $v = \dfrac{\omega}{k}$

$v = \dfrac{314}{31.4} = 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The wavelength is given by $\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{2 \times 3.14}{31.4} = 0.2 \text{ m} = 20 \text{ cm}$

The frequency is given by $f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$

$f = \dfrac{314}{2 \times 3.14} = 50 \text{ Hz}$

Thus, the wave speed is $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, wavelength is $20 \text{ cm}$ and frequency is $50 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave travelling on a string has the equation $y = (0.10 \text{ mm}) \sin[(31.4 \text{ m}^{-1})x + (314 \text{ s}^{-1})t]$. What is the maximum displacement and the maximum speed of a portion of the string?
questions.solution:
The standard equation of a travelling wave is given by $y = A \sin(kx + \omega t)$.

Comparing the given equation $y = (0.10 \text{ mm}) \sin[(31.4 \text{ m}^{-1})x + (314 \text{ s}^{-1})t]$ with the standard equation, we get:
Amplitude $A = 0.10 \text{ mm}$
Angular frequency $\omega = 314 \text{ s}^{-1}$

The maximum displacement of a portion of the string is its amplitude, which is $A = 0.10 \text{ mm}$.

The maximum speed of a portion of the string (maximum particle velocity) is given by $v_{\text{max}} = A\omega$.

Substituting the values:
$v_{\text{max}} = (0.10 \text{ mm}) \times (314 \text{ s}^{-1}) = 31.4 \text{ mm s}^{-1}$

Converting to $\text{cm s}^{-1}$:
$v_{\text{max}} = 3.14 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

Thus, the maximum displacement is $0.10 \text{ mm}$ and the maximum speed is $3.14 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave propagates along the positive $x$-direction with a speed of $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. The amplitude of the wave is $0.20 \text{ cm}$ and the wavelength is $2.0 \text{ cm}$. Which of the following is a possible wave equation that describes this wave?
questions.solution:
The amplitude of the wave is $A = 0.20 \text{ cm}$.

The wavelength is $\lambda = 2.0 \text{ cm}$.

The wave number $k$ is given by $k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2\pi}{2.0 \text{ cm}} = \pi \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

The wave speed is $v = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1} = 2000 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

The angular frequency $\omega$ is given by $\omega = kv = (\pi \text{ cm}^{-1})(2000 \text{ cm s}^{-1}) = 2\pi \times 10^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$.

For a wave propagating in the positive $x$-direction, the equation is of the form $y = A \sin(kx - \omega t)$.

Substituting the values, we get $y = (0.20 \text{ cm}) \sin[(\pi \text{ cm}^{-1})x - (2\pi \times 10^3 \text{ s}^{-1})t]$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave travels along the positive $x$-direction with a speed of $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. The amplitude of the wave is $0.20 \text{ cm}$ and the wavelength is $2.0 \text{ cm}$. Assuming the wave is described by the equation $y = (0.20 \text{ cm}) \sin[(\pi \text{ cm}^{-1})x - (2\pi \times 10^3 \text{ s}^{-1})t]$, determine the displacement and velocity of the particle at $x = 2.0 \text{ cm}$ at time $t = 0$.
options: Displacement is zero, velocity is $-4\pi \text{ m s}^{-1}$
Displacement is zero, velocity is $4\pi \text{ m s}^{-1}$
Displacement is $0.20 \text{ cm}$, velocity is zero
Displacement is $-0.20 \text{ cm}$, velocity is zero
questions.solution:
The given wave equation is $y = 0.20 \sin(\pi x - 2\pi \times 10^3 t)$, where $y$ and $x$ are in cm and $t$ is in s.

Substituting $x = 2.0$ cm and $t = 0$ s into the equation:

$y = 0.20 \sin(\pi \times 2.0 - 0) = 0.20 \sin(2\pi) = 0$

The velocity of the particle is given by the partial derivative of displacement with respect to time:

$v_p = \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial t} [0.20 \sin(\pi x - 2\pi \times 10^3 t)]$

$v_p = 0.20 \times (-2\pi \times 10^3) \cos(\pi x - 2\pi \times 10^3 t)$

$v_p = -400\pi \cos(\pi x - 2\pi \times 10^3 t) \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

Substituting $x = 2.0$ cm and $t = 0$ s:

$v_p = -400\pi \cos(2\pi) = -400\pi \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

Converting to $\text{m s}^{-1}$:

$v_p = -4\pi \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Thus, the displacement is zero and the velocity is $-4\pi \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave is described by the equation $y = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \sin \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{2.0 \text{ cm}} - \dfrac{t}{0.01 \text{ s}}\right)$. Find the time period and the wavelength.
questions.solution:
The given wave equation is $y = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \sin \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{2.0 \text{ cm}} - \dfrac{t}{0.01 \text{ s}}\right)$

Comparing this with the standard wave equation $y = A \sin (kx - \omega t)$, we get:

$k = \dfrac{\pi}{2.0} \text{ cm}^{-1}$

$\omega = \dfrac{\pi}{0.01} \text{ s}^{-1}$

Using the relation $k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$, we find the wavelength:

$\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} = \dfrac{\pi}{2.0} \Rightarrow \lambda = 4.0 \text{ cm}$

Using the relation $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$, we find the time period:

$\dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{\pi}{0.01} \Rightarrow T = 0.02 \text{ s} = 20 \text{ ms}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave is described by the equation $y = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \sin \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{2.0 \text{ cm}} - \dfrac{t}{0.01 \text{ s}}\right)$. Find the speed of the particle at $x = 1.0 \text{ cm}$ at time $t = 0.01 \text{ s}$.
questions.solution:
The given wave equation is:

$y = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \sin \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{2.0 \text{ cm}} - \dfrac{t}{0.01 \text{ s}}\right)$

The particle velocity is given by the partial derivative of displacement with respect to time:

$v_p = \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \cos \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{2.0} - \dfrac{t}{0.01}\right) \times \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{0.01}\right)$

Substituting $x = 1.0 \text{ cm}$ and $t = 0.01 \text{ s}$:

$v_p = -100\pi \cos \pi \left(\dfrac{1.0}{2.0} - \dfrac{0.01}{0.01}\right)$

$v_p = -100\pi \cos \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \pi\right)$

$v_p = -100\pi \cos \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

Since $\cos \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0$, we get:

$v_p = 0$

Thus, the speed of the particle is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave is described by the equation $y = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \sin \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{2.0 \text{ cm}} - \dfrac{t}{0.01 \text{ s}}\right)$. What are the speeds of the particles at $x = 3.0 \text{ cm}$, $5.0 \text{ cm}$ and $7.0 \text{ cm}$ at $t = 0.01 \text{ s}$?
options: $10\pi \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ for all three positions
$5\pi \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ for all three positions
zero, $5\pi \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, and $10\pi \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ respectively
questions.solution:
The given wave equation is $y = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \sin \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{2.0 \text{ cm}} - \dfrac{t}{0.01 \text{ s}}\right)$.

The particle velocity $v_p$ is given by the partial derivative of $y$ with respect to $t$:

$v_p = \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \cos \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{2.0} - \dfrac{t}{0.01}\right) \times \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{0.01}\right)$

Since $1.0 \text{ mm} = 0.1 \text{ cm}$, we get:

$v_p = -10\pi \cos \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{2.0} - \dfrac{t}{0.01}\right) \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

At $t = 0.01 \text{ s}$, the term $\dfrac{t}{0.01} = 1$. Substituting this into the velocity equation:

$v_p = -10\pi \cos \left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2.0} - \pi\right) = 10\pi \cos \left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2.0}\right) \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

Evaluating the particle speed at the given positions:

For $x = 3.0 \text{ cm}$, $v_p = 10\pi \cos \left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = 0$

For $x = 5.0 \text{ cm}$, $v_p = 10\pi \cos \left(\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\right) = 0$

For $x = 7.0 \text{ cm}$, $v_p = 10\pi \cos \left(\dfrac{7\pi}{2}\right) = 0$

Thus, the speeds of the particles are zero for all three positions.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave is described by the equation $y = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \sin \pi \left(\dfrac{x}{2.0 \text{ cm}} - \dfrac{t}{0.01 \text{ s}}\right)$. What are the speeds of the particles at $x = 1.0 \text{ cm}$ at $t = 0.011$, $0.012$, and $0.013 \text{ s}$?
questions.solution:
The given wave equation is $y = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \sin \left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2.0} - 100 \pi t\right)$.

The particle velocity $v$ is given by the partial derivative of $y$ with respect to time $t$:

$v = \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} = (1.0 \text{ mm}) \cos \left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2.0} - 100 \pi t\right) \times (-100 \pi \text{ s}^{-1})$

$v = -100 \pi \cos \left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2.0} - 100 \pi t\right) \text{ mm s}^{-1}$

At $x = 1.0 \text{ cm}$, the argument of the cosine becomes $\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 100 \pi t$. Using $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \sin \theta$, the velocity simplifies to:

$v = -100 \pi \sin(100 \pi t) \text{ mm s}^{-1} = -10 \pi \sin(100 \pi t) \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

The speed is the magnitude of the velocity, $|v| = 10 \pi |\sin(100 \pi t)| \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

At $t = 0.011 \text{ s}$:

$|v| = 10 \pi |\sin(1.1 \pi)| = 10 \pi \sin(18^\circ) = 10 \pi \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4}\right) \approx 9.7 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

At $t = 0.012 \text{ s}$:

$|v| = 10 \pi |\sin(1.2 \pi)| = 10 \pi \sin(36^\circ) = 10 \pi \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{10-2\sqrt{5}}}{4}\right) \approx 18.5 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

At $t = 0.013 \text{ s}$:

$|v| = 10 \pi |\sin(1.3 \pi)| = 10 \pi \sin(54^\circ) = 10 \pi \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{5}+1}{4}\right) \approx 25.4 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

The speeds are approximately $9.7 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, $18 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, and $25 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $9.7 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, $18 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$, $25 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A particle on a stretched string supporting a travelling wave takes $5.0 \text{ ms}$ to travel from its mean position to the extreme position. The distance separating two consecutive particles that are located at their mean positions is $2.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the frequency, the wavelength, and the wave speed.
questions.solution:
The time taken by a particle to travel from its mean position to the extreme position is one-fourth of the time period $T$.

$\dfrac{T}{4} = 5.0 \text{ ms} \Rightarrow T = 20.0 \text{ ms} = 20 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$

The frequency $f$ is given by:

$f = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{20 \times 10^{-3}} = 50 \text{ Hz}$

The distance separating two consecutive particles that are simultaneously at their mean positions corresponds to half of the wavelength $\lambda$.

$\dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 2.0 \text{ cm} \Rightarrow \lambda = 4.0 \text{ cm} = 0.04 \text{ m}$

The wave speed $v$ is the product of frequency and wavelength:

$v = f \lambda = 50 \times 0.04 = 2.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A travelling wave is passing along a string in the positive $x$-direction with a wave speed of $20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. The transverse displacements of the particles of the string at $t = 0$ are plotted in the associated figure. Determine the frequency of the wave.
questions.solution:
From the given displacement-position graph at $t = 0$, the wave completes one full cycle over a distance of $4 \text{ cm}$. Thus, the wavelength of the wave is $\lambda = 4 \text{ cm}$.

The wave speed is given as $v = 20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

The frequency $f$ of the wave is related to the wave speed and wavelength by the formula:

$v = f \lambda$

Substituting the given values, we get:

$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}}{4 \text{ cm}} = 5 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A travelling wave is passing along a string in the positive $x$-direction with a wave speed of $20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. The transverse displacements of the particles of the string at $t = 0$ are plotted in the associated figure. Determine the frequency of the wave.
questions.solution:
The given graph shows the displacement $y$ of the particles of the string as a function of position $x$ at time $t = 0$.

The wavelength $\lambda$ of a wave is the distance over which the wave's shape repeats, which corresponds to the length of one complete cycle.

From the graph, the wave starts a cycle at $x = 0$, crosses the mean position at $x = 2\text{ cm}$ (completing half a cycle), and returns to the same phase at $x = 4\text{ cm}$ (completing one full cycle).

Therefore, the wavelength is $\lambda = 4\text{ cm}$.

questions.q: A wave traveling on a string at a speed of $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ causes each particle of the string to oscillate with a time period of $20 \text{ ms}$. Determine the wavelength of the wave.
questions.solution:
Given, wave speed $v = 10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Time period $T = 20 \text{ ms} = 20 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$

The wavelength $\lambda$ is given by the relation $\lambda = vT$

Substituting the values, we get $\lambda = 10 \times 20 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

$\lambda = 0.2 \text{ m} = 20 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave traveling on a string at a speed of $10 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ causes each particle of the string to oscillate with a time period of $20 \text{ ms}$. If a particle has a displacement of $1.5 \text{ mm}$ at a specific instant, determine the displacement of a particle located $10 \text{ cm}$ away at that identical instant.
questions.solution:
The wavelength of the wave is given by $\lambda = vT$.

Substituting the given values, we get $\lambda = 10 \times 20 \times 10^{-3} = 0.2 \text{ m} = 20 \text{ cm}$.

The phase difference $\Delta \phi$ between two particles separated by a distance $\Delta x$ is $\Delta \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$.

For $\Delta x = 10 \text{ cm}$, the phase difference is $\Delta \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{20} \times 10 = \pi$.

Since the phase difference is $\pi$, the two particles are exactly out of phase. Therefore, their displacements at any instant are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign.

Given the displacement of the first particle is $y_1 = 1.5 \text{ mm}$, the displacement of the second particle is $y_2 = -1.5 \text{ mm}$.

questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A steel wire with a length of $64 \text{ cm}$ weighs $5 \text{ g}$. If it is stretched by an $8 \text{ N}$ force, determine the speed of a transverse wave travelling on it.
questions.solution:
Given, length of the wire $L = 64 \text{ cm} = 0.64 \text{ m}$

Mass of the wire $m = 5 \text{ g} = 5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$

Tension in the wire $T = 8 \text{ N}$

The linear mass density of the wire is given by:

$\mu = \dfrac{m}{L} = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{0.64} = \dfrac{5}{640} = \dfrac{1}{128} \text{ kg/m}$

The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

Substituting the values:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{1/128}} = \sqrt{8 \times 128} = \sqrt{1024} = 32 \text{ m/s}$

questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string of length $20 \text{ cm}$ and linear mass density $0.40 \text{ g cm}^{-1}$ is fixed at both ends and maintained under a tension of $16 \text{ N}$. At $t = 0$, a wave pulse is created near one end, as shown in the figure, and travels towards the other end. At what time will the string again exhibit the shape shown in the figure?
questions.solution:
Given, length of the string, $L = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$
Linear mass density, $\mu = 0.40 \text{ g cm}^{-1} = \dfrac{0.40 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}}{10^{-2} \text{ m}} = 0.04 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$
Tension in the string, $T = 16 \text{ N}$

The speed of the transverse wave pulse on the string is given by:
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{16}{0.04}} = \sqrt{400} = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

For the string to again exhibit the exact same shape (an upright pulse traveling towards the right), the pulse must undergo two reflections.
1. It travels to the right end, reflects, and becomes inverted (since the end is fixed).
2. It travels back to the left end, reflects again, and becomes upright, traveling to the right.

The total distance traveled by the pulse to return to its initial state is $2L$.
Distance $d = 2 \times 0.2 \text{ m} = 0.4 \text{ m}$

The time taken is:
$t = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{0.4}{20} = 0.02 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string with a total length of $30 \text{ cm}$ and a linear mass density of $0.5 \text{ g cm}^{-1}$ is attached to a fixed wall at one end, while its other end is tied to a frictionless ring that is free to slide on a vertical rod, as shown in the figure. A wave pulse is generated on the string, travelling towards the ring at a speed of $20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. The pulse is symmetric around its peak, which is initially situated at a distance of $20 \text{ cm}$ from the ring-joined end. Assuming reflections at the ends occur without any energy loss, determine the time taken by the string to regain its initial shape.
questions.solution:
Given the wave speed $v = 20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ and the initial distance of the pulse peak from the ring is $d = 20 \text{ cm}$.

The time taken by the pulse to reach the ring is $t_1 = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{20}{20} = 1 \text{ s}$.

Since the ring is free to slide, it acts as a free boundary. Reflection at a free boundary occurs without any phase reversal, so the upright pulse reflects as an upright pulse moving in the opposite direction.

For the string to regain its initial spatial shape, the symmetric upright pulse must return to its original position.

The distance traveled back to the initial position is again $d = 20 \text{ cm}$.

The time taken for this return journey is $t_2 = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{20}{20} = 1 \text{ s}$.

The total time taken is $t = t_1 + t_2 = 1 + 1 = 2 \text{ s}$.

A wave pulse is generated on the string, travelling towards the ring at a speed of $20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string of total length $30 \text{ cm}$ and linear mass density $0.5 \text{ g cm}^{-1}$ is secured to a fixed wall at one end and to a frictionless ring on a vertical rod at the other end. A symmetric wave pulse, initially peaking at a distance of $20 \text{ cm}$ from the ring, travels towards the ring at $20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. The reflections at both ends are assumed to be energy lossless. The shape of the string changes periodically with time. Determine this time period.
questions.solution:
For a string of length $L$ secured to a fixed wall at one end and a frictionless ring (free end) at the other, the boundary conditions dictate how a wave pulse reflects:
1. At the free end (ring), the pulse reflects without any phase change (an upright pulse remains upright).
2. At the fixed end (wall), the pulse reflects with a phase change of $\pi$ (an upright pulse becomes inverted).

Let us trace the journey of the initial upright pulse to determine when it returns to its exact initial state (same position, same shape, and same direction of motion):
- The pulse travels towards the free end and reflects. It remains upright but reverses direction.
- It then travels to the fixed end and reflects. It becomes inverted and reverses direction.
- It travels back to the free end and reflects. It remains inverted.
- It travels to the fixed end and reflects again. It becomes upright and reverses direction, now moving in its original direction.

To complete one full cycle and return to its exact initial state, the pulse must undergo two reflections at the free end and two reflections at the fixed end. This corresponds to traveling a total distance of $4L$.

Given:
Length of the string, $L = 30 \text{ cm}$
Wave speed, $v = 20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

The time period $T$ of the periodic change in the shape of the string is the time taken to travel this total distance of $4L$:

$T = \dfrac{4L}{v}$

Substituting the given values:

$T = \dfrac{4 \times 30 \text{ cm}}{20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}} = \dfrac{120}{20} \text{ s} = 6 \text{ s}$

Answer: $6 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: One end of a string having a total length of $30 \text{ cm}$ and a linear mass density of $0.5 \text{ g cm}^{-1}$ is fixed to a wall, and the other end is attached to a frictionless ring that slides on a vertical rod. A wave pulse moves along the string towards the ring at a speed of $20 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. The pulse is symmetric about its maximum, initially located $20 \text{ cm}$ from the ring. Assuming no energy is lost during reflections at the ends, what is the tension in the string?
questions.solution:
Given, linear mass density of the string, $\mu = 0.5 \text{ g cm}^{-1}$.
Converting to SI units:
$\mu = \dfrac{0.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}}{10^{-2} \text{ m}} = 0.05 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$

Speed of the wave pulse, $v = 20 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 0.2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is given by the relation:
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

Rearranging the formula to solve for tension $T$:
$T = \mu v^2$

Substituting the given values:
$T = 0.05 \times (0.2)^2$
$T = 0.05 \times 0.04$
$T = 0.002 \text{ N} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: Two wires possessing different densities but the same area of cross section are joined together at one end and stretched to a tension $T$. The velocity of a transverse wave in the first wire is twice that in the second wire. Determine the ratio of the density of the first wire to the density of the second wire.
questions.solution:
The velocity of a transverse wave in a stretched wire is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$, where $\mu$ is the linear mass density.

Since $\mu = \rho A$, where $\rho$ is the density and $A$ is the cross-sectional area, the velocity can be written as $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\rho A}}$.

For the two wires, the tension $T$ and area $A$ are the same. Thus, $v \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\rho}}$.

Given that $v_1 = 2v_2$, we have:

$\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\rho_1 A}} = 2 \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\rho_2 A}}$

Squaring both sides:

$\dfrac{T}{\rho_1 A} = 4 \dfrac{T}{\rho_2 A}$

$\dfrac{1}{\rho_1} = \dfrac{4}{\rho_2}$

$\dfrac{\rho_1}{\rho_2} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A transverse wave given by $y = (0.02 \text{ m}) \sin[(1.0 \text{ m}^{-1})x + (30 \text{ s}^{-1})t]$ propagates along a stretched string with a linear mass density of $1.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg m}^{-1}$. Determine the tension in the string.
questions.solution:
Comparing the given equation $y = 0.02 \sin(x + 30t)$ with the standard wave equation $y = A \sin(kx + \omega t)$, we get:

$k = 1.0 \text{ m}^{-1}$

$\omega = 30 \text{ s}^{-1}$

The wave speed $v$ is given by:

$v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} = \dfrac{30}{1.0} = 30 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The wave speed on a stretched string is related to tension $T$ and linear mass density $\mu$ by:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} \Rightarrow T = \mu v^2$

Given $\mu = 1.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ kg m}^{-1}$, substituting the values:

$T = (1.2 \times 10^{-4}) \times (30)^2$

$T = 1.2 \times 10^{-4} \times 900$

$T = 1080 \times 10^{-4} = 0.108 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: By sinusoidally vibrating one end of a long horizontal string up and down, a travelling wave is generated. The vibration amplitude is $1.0 \text{ cm}$, and the displacement reaches zero $200$ times per second. The string has a linear mass density of $0.10 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$ and is maintained under a tension of $90 \text{ N}$. Find the speed and the wavelength of the wave.
questions.solution:
The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is given by the formula:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

Substituting the given values of tension $T = 90 \text{ N}$ and linear mass density $\mu = 0.10 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{90}{0.10}} = \sqrt{900} = 30 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

In a sinusoidal wave, the displacement of any particle on the string becomes zero twice during each complete cycle. Since the displacement reaches zero $200$ times per second, the frequency $f$ of the wave is:

$f = \dfrac{200}{2} = 100 \text{ Hz}$

The wavelength $\lambda$ is related to the wave speed and frequency by the equation $v = f \lambda$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{30}{100} = 0.30 \text{ m} = 30 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: By sinusoidally vibrating one end of a long horizontal string up and down, a travelling wave is generated. The vibration amplitude is $1.0 \text{ cm}$, and the displacement reaches zero $200$ times per second. The string has a linear mass density of $0.10 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$ and is maintained under a tension of $90 \text{ N}$. Assuming the wave travels in the positive $x$-direction and the end at $x = 0$ is at its positive extreme position at $t = 0$, determine the wave equation.
questions.solution:
The amplitude of the wave is given as $A = 1.0 \text{ cm}$.

Since the displacement of a particle in simple harmonic motion reaches zero twice in one complete cycle, the frequency $f$ of the wave is:

$f = \dfrac{200}{2} = 100 \text{ Hz}$

The time period $T$ is:

$T = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{100} = 0.01 \text{ s}$

The wave speed $v$ is determined by the tension $F$ and the linear mass density $\mu$:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{F}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{90}{0.10}} = \sqrt{900} = 30 \text{ m s}^{-1} = 3000 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$

The wavelength $\lambda$ is:

$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{3000}{100} = 30 \text{ cm}$

The general equation for a wave travelling in the positive $x$-direction is:

$y(x,t) = A \cos\left(2\pi \left(\dfrac{x}{\lambda} - \dfrac{t}{T}\right) + \phi\right)$

At $x = 0$ and $t = 0$, the displacement is at its positive extreme, so $y(0,0) = A$. This gives $\cos(\phi) = 1$, which implies $\phi = 0$.

Substituting the values of $A$, $\lambda$, and $T$, we get:

$y = (1.0 \text{ cm}) \cos 2\pi \left[\dfrac{x}{30 \text{ cm}} - \dfrac{t}{0.01 \text{ s}}\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: By sinusoidally vibrating one end of a long horizontal string up and down, a travelling wave is generated. The vibration amplitude is $1.0 \text{ cm}$, and the displacement reaches zero $200$ times per second. The string has a linear mass density of $0.10 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$ and is maintained under a tension of $90 \text{ N}$. The wave propagates in the positive $x$-direction, and at $t = 0$, the end at $x = 0$ is at its positive extreme position. Determine the velocity and acceleration of the particle at $x = 50 \text{ cm}$ at time $t = 10 \text{ ms}$.
questions.solution:
Given the amplitude $A = 1.0 \text{ cm} = 0.01 \text{ m}$.

Since the displacement reaches zero $200$ times per second and a sinusoidal wave crosses zero twice per cycle, the frequency is $f = \dfrac{200}{2} = 100 \text{ Hz}$.

The angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi f = 200\pi \text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

The wave speed is given by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{90}{0.10}} = 30 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The wave number is $k = \dfrac{\omega}{v} = \dfrac{200\pi}{30} = \dfrac{20\pi}{3} \text{ m}^{-1}$.

The wave propagates in the positive $x$-direction. At $t = 0$ and $x = 0$, the particle is at its positive extreme, so the wave equation is $y(x,t) = A \cos(\omega t - kx)$.

We need to find the velocity and acceleration at $x = 50 \text{ cm} = 0.5 \text{ m}$ and $t = 10 \text{ ms} = 0.01 \text{ s}$.

The phase angle is $\theta = \omega t - kx = (200\pi)(0.01) - \left(\dfrac{20\pi}{3}\right)(0.5) = 2\pi - \dfrac{10\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$.

The particle velocity is $v_p = \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t} = -A\omega \sin(\omega t - kx)$.

Substituting the values, $v_p = -(0.01)(200\pi) \sin\left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) = -2\pi \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -\sqrt{3}\pi \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The particle acceleration is $a_p = \dfrac{\partial^2 y}{\partial t^2} = -A\omega^2 \cos(\omega t - kx)$.

Substituting the values, $a_p = -(0.01)(200\pi)^2 \cos\left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) = -400\pi^2 \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 200\pi^2 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string of length $40 \text{ cm}$ and weighing $10 \text{ g}$ is connected to a spring at one end and to a fixed wall at its other end. The spring possesses a spring constant of $160 \text{ N m}^{-1}$ and is stretched by $1.0 \text{ cm}$. If a wave pulse is generated on the string near the wall, determine the time it will take to reach the spring.
questions.solution:
The tension in the string is provided by the restoring force of the stretched spring.

$T = kx = 160 \times 0.01 = 1.6 \text{ N}$

The linear mass density of the string is:

$\mu = \dfrac{m}{L} = \dfrac{10 \times 10^{-3}}{40 \times 10^{-2}} = 0.025 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$

The speed of the transverse wave on the string is given by:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1.6}{0.025}} = \sqrt{64} = 8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The time taken by the wave pulse to travel the length of the string is:

$t = \dfrac{L}{v} = \dfrac{0.4}{8} = 0.05 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: As shown in the figure, two blocks, each with a mass of $3.2 \text{ kg}$, are connected by a wire $CD$. The entire system is suspended from the ceiling using another wire $AB$. The linear mass density of wire $AB$ is $10 \text{ g m}^{-1}$, while that of wire $CD$ is $8 \text{ g m}^{-1}$. Determine the speed of a transverse wave pulse produced in $AB$ and in $CD$.
questions.solution:
Given:
Mass of each block, $m = 3.2 \text{ kg}$
Linear mass density of wire $AB$, $\mu_{AB} = 10 \text{ g m}^{-1} = 0.01 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$
Linear mass density of wire $CD$, $\mu_{CD} = 8 \text{ g m}^{-1} = 0.008 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$
Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 9.8 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

The tension in wire $CD$ is provided by the weight of the lower block:
$T_{CD} = mg = 3.2 \times 9.8 = 31.36 \text{ N}$

The speed of the transverse wave pulse in $CD$ is:
$v_{CD} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_{CD}}{\mu_{CD}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{31.36}{0.008}} = \sqrt{3920} \approx 62.6 \text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 63 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The tension in wire $AB$ is provided by the weight of both blocks (neglecting the mass of the wires):
$T_{AB} = 2mg = 2 \times 3.2 \times 9.8 = 62.72 \text{ N}$

The speed of the transverse wave pulse in $AB$ is:
$v_{AB} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_{AB}}{\mu_{AB}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{62.72}{0.01}} = \sqrt{6272} \approx 79.2 \text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 79 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Thus, the speeds in $AB$ and $CD$ are $79 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $63 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ respectively.

questions.q: For the arrangement shown in the figure, the string has a mass of $4.5 \text{ g}$. Calculate the time required for a transverse disturbance generated at the floor to reach the pulley. Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
The total length of the string is the sum of the lengths on both sides of the pulley.

$l = 2.0 \text{ m} + 0.25 \text{ m} = 2.25 \text{ m}$

The mass of the string is given as $m = 4.5 \text{ g} = 4.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$.

The linear mass density $\mu$ of the string is:

$\mu = \dfrac{m}{l} = \dfrac{4.5 \times 10^{-3}}{2.25} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg/m}$

The tension $T$ in the string is provided by the weight of the suspended block. Since the mass of the string is negligible compared to the block, the tension is uniform throughout the string.

$T = Mg = 2 \times 10 = 20 \text{ N}$

The speed $v$ of the transverse wave in the string is:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{2 \times 10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{10000} = 100 \text{ m/s}$

The distance $d$ from the floor to the pulley is $2.0 \text{ m}$. The time $t$ required for the disturbance to reach the pulley is:

$t = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{2.0}{100} = 0.02 \text{ s}$

questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A $4.0 \text{ kg}$ block is suspended from the ceiling of an elevator by a string with a linear mass density of $19.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg m}^{-1}$. Determine the speed (relative to the string) at which a wave pulse can travel along the string, given that the elevator accelerates upward at a rate of $2.0 \text{ m s}^{-2}$. Use $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
The effective acceleration of the block in the elevator accelerating upward is given by:

$g_{\text{eff}} = g + a = 10 + 2.0 = 12.0 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

The tension in the string is equal to the apparent weight of the suspended block:

$T = M g_{\text{eff}} = 4.0 \times 12.0 = 48 \text{ N}$

The speed of a transverse wave pulse on a string is given by the formula:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

Substituting the given values:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{48}{19.2 \times 10^{-3}}}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{48000}{19.2}} = \sqrt{2500}$

$v = 50 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A heavy ball hangs from the ceiling of a motor car by a light string. When the car is stationary, a transverse pulse travels on the string at a speed of $60 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. When the car accelerates along a horizontal road, the pulse travels at $62 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. Determine the acceleration of the car. Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
Let $m$ be the mass of the heavy ball and $\mu$ be the mass per unit length of the string.

When the car is stationary, the tension in the string is $T_1 = mg$.

The speed of the transverse pulse is given by $v_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_1}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{mg}{\mu}} = 60 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

When the car accelerates horizontally with acceleration $a$, the effective acceleration due to gravity becomes $g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + a^2}$.

The new tension in the string is $T_2 = m\sqrt{g^2 + a^2}$.

The new speed of the transverse pulse is $v_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m\sqrt{g^2 + a^2}}{\mu}} = 62 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

Taking the ratio of the speeds:

$\dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sqrt{g^2 + a^2}}{g}} = \left(1 + \dfrac{a^2}{g^2}\right)^{1/4}$

Substituting the given values:

$\left(\dfrac{62}{60}\right)^4 = 1 + \dfrac{a^2}{g^2}$

$\left(\dfrac{31}{30}\right)^4 = 1 + \dfrac{a^2}{10^2}$

$1.140 \approx 1 + \dfrac{a^2}{100}$

$\dfrac{a^2}{100} \approx 0.140$

$a^2 \approx 14.0$

$a = \sqrt{14.0} \approx 3.74 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A circular loop of string is rotating about its axis on a frictionless horizontal plane at a uniform rate, ensuring that the tangential speed of any particle of the string is $v$. When a small transverse disturbance is generated at a point on the loop, at what speed (relative to the string) does this disturbance propagate along the string?
questions.solution:
Consider a small element of the string subtending an angle $d\theta$ at the center of the circular loop.

Let the radius of the loop be $R$ and the mass per unit length of the string be $\mu$.

The mass of this small element is $dm = \mu R d\theta$.

The element is rotating in a circle of radius $R$ with a constant tangential speed $v$. The centripetal force required for this circular motion is provided by the inward component of the tension $T$ at the two ends of the element.

The net inward force is $2T \sin\left(\dfrac{d\theta}{2}\right) \approx T d\theta$ since $d\theta$ is very small.

Equating this to the required centripetal force:

$T d\theta = \dfrac{(dm) v^2}{R}$

$T d\theta = \dfrac{(\mu R d\theta) v^2}{R}$

$T = \mu v^2$

The speed of a transverse wave propagating along a string under tension $T$ is given by:

$c = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

Substituting $T = \mu v^2$, we get:

$c = \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu v^2}{\mu}} = v$

Thus, the speed of the disturbance relative to the string is $v$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A heavy but uniform rope of length $L$ is suspended from a ceiling. Determine the velocity of a transverse wave travelling on the string as a function of the distance $x$ from the lower end.
questions.solution:
Let the mass per unit length of the rope be $\mu$.

The tension $T$ at a distance $x$ from the lower end is equal to the weight of the rope below that point.

$T = \mu x g$

The velocity $v$ of a transverse wave on a string is given by:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

Substituting the value of $T$, we get:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu x g}{\mu}} = \sqrt{gx}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A heavy but uniform rope of length $L$ is suspended from a ceiling. If the rope is given a sudden sideways jerk at the bottom, how long will it take for the pulse to reach the ceiling?
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the rope be $M$ and its length be $L$. The linear mass density is $\mu = \dfrac{M}{L}$.

Consider a point at a distance $x$ from the bottom of the rope. The tension $T$ at this point is due to the weight of the rope below it.

$T = (\mu x) g$

The speed of the transverse pulse at a distance $x$ from the bottom is given by:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu x g}{\mu}} = \sqrt{gx}$

Since $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$, we have:

$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \sqrt{gx}$

$dt = \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{gx}}$

Integrating both sides to find the total time $t$ taken by the pulse to travel from the bottom ($x = 0$) to the ceiling ($x = L$):

$t = \int_{0}^{L} \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{gx}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{g}} \int_{0}^{L} x^{-1/2} dx$

$t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{g}} \left[ 2\sqrt{x} \right]_{0}^{L} = 2\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4L}{g}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A heavy but uniform rope of length $L$ is suspended from a ceiling. A particle is dropped from the ceiling at the exact instant the bottom end of the rope is given a sudden sideways jerk. At what location will the particle meet the resulting pulse?
options: At a distance $\dfrac{L}{4}$ from the bottom
At a distance $\dfrac{L}{2}$ from the bottom
At a distance $\dfrac{2L}{3}$ from the bottom
At a distance $\dfrac{L}{3}$ from the bottom
questions.solution:
Let $x$ be the distance of the pulse from the bottom of the rope at time $t$.

The tension in the rope at a distance $x$ from the bottom is $T = \mu g x$, where $\mu$ is the mass per unit length of the rope.

The speed of the transverse pulse is $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{g x}$.

Since $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$, we have $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \sqrt{g x}$.

Rearranging and integrating from $t = 0$ to $t$:

$\int_{0}^{x} x^{-1/2} dx = \int_{0}^{t} \sqrt{g} dt$

$2\sqrt{x} = \sqrt{g} t \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{g t^2}{4}$

At the same time $t$, the distance fallen by the particle dropped from the ceiling is $y = \dfrac{1}{2} g t^2$.

Comparing $x$ and $y$, we get $y = 2x$.

The particle and the pulse meet when the sum of their distances equals the total length of the rope $L$:

$x + y = L$

$x + 2x = L$

$3x = L \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{L}{3}$

Thus, they meet at a distance $\dfrac{L}{3}$ from the bottom.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: Two long strings, $A$ and $B$, each possessing a linear mass density of $1.2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ kg m}^{-1}$, are stretched by tensions of $4.8 \text{ N}$ and $7.5 \text{ N}$ respectively. They are kept parallel to each other with their left ends positioned at $x = 0$. Wave pulses are initiated at these left ends at $t = 0$ on string $A$ and at $t = 20 \text{ ms}$ on string $B$. Determine when and where the pulse on string $B$ overtakes the pulse on string $A$.
questions.solution:
The velocity of the wave pulse on string A is given by

$v_A = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_A}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4.8}{1.2 \times 10^{-2}}} = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The velocity of the wave pulse on string B is given by

$v_B = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_B}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7.5}{1.2 \times 10^{-2}}} = 25 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Let the pulse on string B overtake the pulse on string A at time $t$. The distance traveled by the pulse on string A in time $t$ is

$x_A = v_A t = 20t$

The pulse on string B starts at $t = 20 \text{ ms} = 0.02 \text{ s}$. The distance traveled by the pulse on string B is

$x_B = v_B (t - 0.02) = 25(t - 0.02)$

Since both pulses meet at the same position, we equate $x_A$ and $x_B$:

$20t = 25(t - 0.02)$

$20t = 25t - 0.5$

$5t = 0.5$

$t = 0.1 \text{ s} = 100 \text{ ms}$

The position where they meet is

$x = 20 \times 0.1 = 2.0 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A transverse wave with an amplitude of $0.50 \text{ mm}$ and a frequency of $100 \text{ Hz}$ is generated on a wire stretched under a tension of $100 \text{ N}$. Given that the wave speed is $100 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, determine the average power transmitted to the wire by the source.
questions.solution:
The average power transmitted by a transverse wave on a stretched string is given by:

$P_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu \omega^2 A^2 v$

The wave speed is related to tension and linear mass density by $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$, which gives $\mu = \dfrac{T}{v^2}$.

Substituting $\mu$ into the power equation:

$P_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{T}{v^2} \right) \omega^2 A^2 v = \dfrac{T \omega^2 A^2}{2v}$

Given values are:
$T = 100 \text{ N}$
$v = 100 \text{ m s}^{-1}$
$f = 100 \text{ Hz} \Rightarrow \omega = 2 \pi f = 200 \pi \text{ rad s}^{-1}$
$A = 0.50 \text{ mm} = 0.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

Substituting these values:

$P_{avg} = \dfrac{100 \times (200 \pi)^2 \times (0.5 \times 10^{-3})^2}{2 \times 100}$

$P_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 40000 \pi^2 \times 0.25 \times 10^{-6}$

$P_{avg} = 5000 \pi^2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ W}$

$P_{avg} = 5 \pi^2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ W}$

Using $\pi^2 \approx 9.87$:

$P_{avg} \approx 5 \times 9.87 \times 10^{-3} \text{ W} = 49.35 \text{ mW}$

The closest value is $49 \text{ mW}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave with a frequency of $200 \text{ Hz}$ and an amplitude of $1 \text{ mm}$ travels on a long string. The string has a linear mass density of $6 \text{ g m}^{-1}$ and is subjected to a tension of $60 \text{ N}$. Determine the average power transmitted across a given point on the string.
questions.solution:
Given:
Frequency $f = 200 \text{ Hz}$
Amplitude $A = 1 \text{ mm} = 10^{-3} \text{ m}$
Linear mass density $\mu = 6 \text{ g m}^{-1} = 6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg m}^{-1}$
Tension $T = 60 \text{ N}$

The wave speed $v$ is given by:
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{60}{6 \times 10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{10000} = 100 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The angular frequency $\omega$ is:
$\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 200 = 400\pi \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

The average power transmitted across a given point on the string is:
$P_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu v \omega^2 A^2$

Substituting the values:
$P_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (6 \times 10^{-3}) \times 100 \times (400\pi)^2 \times (10^{-3})^2$

$P_{avg} = 0.3 \times 160000\pi^2 \times 10^{-6}$

$P_{avg} = 0.048 \pi^2$

Using $\pi^2 \approx 9.87$:
$P_{avg} \approx 0.048 \times 9.87 \approx 0.47 \text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wave with a frequency of $200 \text{ Hz}$ and an amplitude of $1 \text{ mm}$ travels on a long string. The string has a linear mass density of $6 \text{ g m}^{-1}$ and is subjected to a tension of $60 \text{ N}$. Determine the total energy associated with the wave in a $2.0 \text{ m}$ long portion of the string.
questions.solution:
Given:
Frequency, $f = 200 \text{ Hz}$
Amplitude, $A = 1 \text{ mm} = 10^{-3} \text{ m}$
Linear mass density, $\mu = 6 \text{ g m}^{-1} = 6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg m}^{-1}$
Length of the string, $L = 2.0 \text{ m}$
Tension, $T = 60 \text{ N}$

The wave speed is $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{60}{6 \times 10^{-3}}} = 100 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
The wavelength is $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{100}{200} = 0.5 \text{ m}$.
Since $L = 2.0 \text{ m} = 4\lambda$, the length is an integer multiple of the wavelength, so the average energy density formula can be used exactly.

The total energy $E$ of the wave in a length $L$ is given by:
$E = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu \omega^2 A^2 L$

Substituting $\omega = 2 \pi f$:
$E = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu (2 \pi f)^2 A^2 L$
$E = 2 \pi^2 \mu f^2 A^2 L$

Substituting the given values:
$E = 2 \pi^2 (6 \times 10^{-3}) (200)^2 (10^{-3})^2 (2.0)$
$E = 2 \pi^2 \times 6 \times 10^{-3} \times 40000 \times 10^{-6} \times 2.0$
$E = 9.6 \pi^2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}$

Using $\pi^2 \approx 9.87$:
$E \approx 9.6 \times 9.87 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}$
$E \approx 94.75 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}$
$E \approx 9.475 \times 10^{-3} \text{ J} \approx 9.5 \text{ mJ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A tuning fork with a frequency of $440 \text{ Hz}$ is connected to a long string having a linear mass density of $0.01 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$ and maintained under a tension of $49 \text{ N}$. The tuning fork generates transverse waves with an amplitude of $0.50 \text{ mm}$ along the string. Determine the wave speed and the wavelength of these waves.
questions.solution:
Given parameters are:

Frequency, $f = 440 \text{ Hz}$

Linear mass density, $\mu = 0.01 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$

Tension, $T = 49 \text{ N}$

The wave speed $v$ on a stretched string is given by:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

Substituting the given values:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{49}{0.01}} = \sqrt{4900} = 70 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The wavelength $\lambda$ is related to the wave speed and frequency by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$

Substituting the values:

$\lambda = \dfrac{70}{440} \text{ m} = \dfrac{7}{44} \text{ m}$

Converting to centimeters:

$\lambda = \dfrac{700}{44} \text{ cm} \approx 15.9 \text{ cm} \approx 16 \text{ cm}$

The wave speed is $70 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the wavelength is $16 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A tuning fork with a frequency of $440 \text{ Hz}$ is connected to a long string having a linear mass density of $0.01 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$ and maintained under a tension of $49 \text{ N}$. The tuning fork generates transverse waves with an amplitude of $0.50 \text{ mm}$ along the string. Determine the maximum speed and acceleration of a particle on the string.
questions.solution:
Given:
Frequency of the tuning fork, $f = 440 \text{ Hz}$
Amplitude of the transverse wave, $A = 0.50 \text{ mm} = 0.50 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

The angular frequency of the wave is:
$\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 440 = 880\pi \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

The maximum speed of a particle on the string is given by:
$v_{\text{max}} = A\omega$
$v_{\text{max}} = (0.50 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}) \times (880\pi \text{ rad s}^{-1}) = 0.44\pi \text{ m s}^{-1}$
$v_{\text{max}} \approx 1.38 \text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 1.4 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The maximum acceleration of a particle on the string is given by:
$a_{\text{max}} = A\omega^2$
$a_{\text{max}} = v_{\text{max}}\omega = 0.44\pi \times 880\pi \approx 3824 \text{ m s}^{-2}$
$a_{\text{max}} \approx 3.8 \text{ km s}^{-2}$

The values of tension and linear mass density are not required to find the maximum speed and acceleration of the particle.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A tuning fork with a frequency of $440 \text{ Hz}$ is connected to a long string having a linear mass density of $0.01 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$ and maintained under a tension of $49 \text{ N}$. The tuning fork generates transverse waves with an amplitude of $0.50 \text{ mm}$ along the string. Determine the average rate at which the tuning fork transmits energy to the string.
questions.solution:
Given:
Frequency $f = 440 \text{ Hz}$
Linear mass density $\mu = 0.01 \text{ kg m}^{-1}$
Tension $T = 49 \text{ N}$
Amplitude $A = 0.50 \text{ mm} = 0.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

The wave speed $v$ is given by:
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{49}{0.01}} = 70 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The angular frequency $\omega$ is:
$\omega = 2 \pi f = 2 \pi \times 440 = 880 \pi \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

The average rate at which energy is transmitted (average power) is:
$P_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu v \omega^2 A^2$

Substituting the values:
$P_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.01 \times 70 \times (880 \pi)^2 \times (0.5 \times 10^{-3})^2$

$P_{avg} = 0.35 \times 774400 \pi^2 \times 0.25 \times 10^{-6}$

$P_{avg} = 0.06776 \pi^2$

Using $\pi^2 \approx 9.87$:
$P_{avg} \approx 0.06776 \times 9.87 \approx 0.67 \text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: Two waves propagating in the same direction through the same region possess equal frequencies, wavelengths, and amplitudes. If each wave has an amplitude of $4 \text{ mm}$ and the phase difference between the waves is $90^\circ$, what is the resultant amplitude?
questions.solution:
The resultant amplitude $A_R$ of two waves with amplitudes $A_1$ and $A_2$ and a phase difference $\phi$ is given by:

$A_R = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2 \cos\phi}$

Given $A_1 = A_2 = 4 \text{ mm}$ and $\phi = 90^\circ$.

Substituting the values:

$A_R = \sqrt{4^2 + 4^2 + 2(4)(4) \cos 90^\circ}$

Since $\cos 90^\circ = 0$:

$A_R = \sqrt{16 + 16 + 0} = \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2} \text{ mm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: The figure displays two wave pulses on a string at $t = 0$, travelling in opposite directions with an identical wave speed of $50 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$. Among the times $t = 4 \text{ ms}$, $6 \text{ ms}$, $8 \text{ ms}$, and $12 \text{ ms}$, at which instant will the string have zero displacement everywhere?
questions.solution:
The initial position of the first wave pulse (positive displacement) is from $x = 2 \text{ mm}$ to $x = 6 \text{ mm}$. It is travelling in the positive x-direction.

The initial position of the second wave pulse (negative displacement) is from $x = 10 \text{ mm}$ to $x = 14 \text{ mm}$. It is travelling in the negative x-direction.

The wave speed is given as $v = 50 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 500 \text{ mm s}^{-1}$.

At any time $t$, the position of the first pulse is $[2 + vt, 6 + vt]$ and the position of the second pulse is $[10 - vt, 14 - vt]$.

For the string to have zero displacement everywhere, the positive pulse must completely overlap with the negative pulse. This requires their positions to be identical:

$2 + vt = 10 - vt$

$2vt = 8 \implies vt = 4 \text{ mm}$

Substituting the value of $v$:

$500 \times t = 4$

$t = \dfrac{4}{500} \text{ s} = 0.008 \text{ s}$

Converting to milliseconds:

$t = 8 \text{ ms}$

At $t = 8 \text{ ms}$, both pulses exactly overlap between $x = 6 \text{ mm}$ and $x = 10 \text{ mm}$, cancelling each other out completely.

Among the times $t = 4 \text{ ms}$, $6 \text{ ms}$, $8 \text{ ms}$, and $12 \text{ ms}$, at which instant will the string have zero displacement everywhere?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q:
Two waves, each possessing a frequency of $100 \text{ Hz}$, a wavelength of $2.0 \text{ cm}$, and an amplitude of $2.0 \text{ mm}$, travel in the same direction on a string. Determine the phase difference and the resultant wave amplitude for the following two scenarios:

First scenario: The second wave is produced $0.015 \text{ s}$ later than the first wave at the identical location.
Second scenario: Both waves are produced simultaneously, while the first wave is generated at a distance of $4.0 \text{ cm}$ behind the second wave.

Identify the correct values of (phase difference, resultant amplitude) for the first and second scenarios, respectively.
options: First scenario: $4\pi \text{ rad}$, $4.0 \text{ mm}$; Second scenario: $3\pi \text{ rad}$, $0 \text{ mm}$
First scenario: $3\pi \text{ rad}$, $4.0 \text{ mm}$; Second scenario: $4\pi \text{ rad}$, $0 \text{ mm}$
First scenario: $1.5\pi \text{ rad}$, $0 \text{ mm}$; Second scenario: $2\pi \text{ rad}$, $4.0 \text{ mm}$
First scenario: $3\pi \text{ rad}$, $0 \text{ mm}$; Second scenario: $4\pi \text{ rad}$, $4.0 \text{ mm}$
questions.solution:
Given $f = 100 \text{ Hz}$, $\lambda = 2.0 \text{ cm}$, $A = 2.0 \text{ mm}$.

For the first scenario, the time difference is $\Delta t = 0.015 \text{ s}$.
The phase difference due to the time difference is $\Delta \phi_1 = 2\pi f \Delta t$.
$\Delta \phi_1 = 2\pi \times 100 \times 0.015 = 3\pi \text{ rad}$
The resultant amplitude is $A_{R1} = \sqrt{A^2 + A^2 + 2A^2 \cos(\Delta \phi_1)}$.
$A_{R1} = \sqrt{2A^2 + 2A^2 \cos(3\pi)} = \sqrt{2A^2 - 2A^2} = 0 \text{ mm}$

For the second scenario, the path difference is $\Delta x = 4.0 \text{ cm}$.
The phase difference due to the path difference is $\Delta \phi_2 = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$.
$\Delta \phi_2 = \dfrac{2\pi}{2.0} \times 4.0 = 4\pi \text{ rad}$
The resultant amplitude is $A_{R2} = \sqrt{A^2 + A^2 + 2A^2 \cos(\Delta \phi_2)}$.
$A_{R2} = \sqrt{2A^2 + 2A^2 \cos(4\pi)} = \sqrt{4A^2} = 2A = 4.0 \text{ mm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: Determine the fundamental frequency of vibration if the speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string of length $1 \text{ m}$ is $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of a stretched string fixed at both ends is given by $f = \dfrac{v}{2L}$, where $v$ is the speed of the transverse wave and $L$ is the length of the string.

Given $v = 60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $L = 1 \text{ m}$.

Substituting the values, we get $f = \dfrac{60}{2 \times 1} = 30 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wire of length $2.00 \text{ m}$ is subjected to a tension of $160 \text{ N}$. Determine the linear mass density of the wire if its fundamental frequency of vibration is $100 \text{ Hz}$.
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of a stretched wire is given by:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

where $L$ is the length, $T$ is the tension, and $\mu$ is the linear mass density.

Rearranging the formula to solve for $\mu$:

$\mu = \dfrac{T}{(2Lf)^2}$

Substituting the given values $L = 2.00 \text{ m}$, $T = 160 \text{ N}$, and $f = 100 \text{ Hz}$:

$\mu = \dfrac{160}{(2 \times 2.00 \times 100)^2}$

$\mu = \dfrac{160}{(400)^2}$

$\mu = \dfrac{160}{160000}$

$\mu = 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg/m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A steel wire with a mass of $4.0 \text{ g}$ and a length of $80 \text{ cm}$ is fixed at both its ends. The tension in the wire is $50 \text{ N}$. Determine the frequency and wavelength of the fourth harmonic of the fundamental.
questions.solution:
Linear mass density of the wire is $\mu = \dfrac{m}{L} = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}{0.8} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg/m}$

The speed of the transverse wave on the string is $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{50}{5.0 \times 10^{-3}}} = 100 \text{ m/s}$

For a string fixed at both ends, the frequency of the $n$-th harmonic is given by $f_n = \dfrac{nv}{2L}$

For the fourth harmonic, $n = 4$

$f_4 = \dfrac{4 \times 100}{2 \times 0.8} = 250 \text{ Hz}$

The wavelength of the $n$-th harmonic is given by $\lambda_n = \dfrac{2L}{n}$

$\lambda_4 = \dfrac{2 \times 80}{4} = 40 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A piano wire weighing $6.00 \text{ g}$ and having a length of $90.0 \text{ cm}$ produces a fundamental frequency corresponding to "Middle C" ($\nu = 261.63 \text{ Hz}$). Determine the tension in the wire.
questions.solution:
Mass of the wire, $m = 6.00 ext{ g} = 6 imes 10^{-3} ext{ kg}$

Length of the wire, $L = 90.0 ext{ cm} = 0.9 ext{ m}$

Fundamental frequency, $ u = 261.63 ext{ Hz}$

The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is given by:

$ u = \dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

where $\mu = \dfrac{m}{L}$ is the linear mass density.

Squaring both sides and rearranging for tension $T$:

$T = 4 L^2 u^2 \mu = 4 L m u^2$

Substituting the given values:

$T = 4 imes 0.9 imes 6 imes 10^{-3} imes (261.63)^2$

$T = 0.0216 imes 68450.26$

$T \approx 1478.5 ext{ N}$

Rounding off to three significant figures, we get:

$T = 1480 ext{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: Vibrating in its second harmonic, a sonometer wire with a length of $1.50 \text{ m}$ between the bridges is in resonance with a tuning fork of frequency $256 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the speed of the transverse wave on the wire.
questions.solution:
Given length of the wire, $L = 1.50 \text{ m}$ and frequency, $f = 256 \text{ Hz}$.

For a wire vibrating in its second harmonic ($n = 2$), the frequency is given by $f = \dfrac{n v}{2 L}$.

Substituting $n = 2$, we get $f = \dfrac{2 v}{2 L} = \dfrac{v}{L}$.

The speed of the transverse wave is $v = f L$.

Substituting the given values, $v = 256 \times 1.50 = 384 \text{ m/s}$.

questions.q: The length of the wire between the pulleys, as shown in the figure, is $1.5 \text{ m}$, and its mass is $12.0 \text{ g}$. Determine the frequency of vibration when the wire vibrates in two loops, leaving the middle point of the wire between the pulleys at rest.
questions.solution:
Given:
Length of the wire, $L = 1.5 \text{ m}$
Mass of the wire, $m = 12.0 \text{ g} = 12 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$
Mass of the hanging blocks, $M = 9 \text{ kg}$

The linear mass density of the wire is:
$\mu = \dfrac{m}{L} = \dfrac{12 \times 10^{-3}}{1.5} = 8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg/m}$

The tension in the wire is provided by the hanging mass (taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$):
$T = Mg = 9 \times 9.8 = 88.2 \text{ N}$

The speed of the transverse wave in the wire is:
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{88.2}{8 \times 10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{11025} = 105 \text{ m/s}$

Since the wire vibrates in two loops, there is a node at the center. The length of the wire corresponds to two half-wavelengths:
$L = 2 \left(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\right) \Rightarrow \lambda = L = 1.5 \text{ m}$

The frequency of vibration is:
$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{105}{1.5} = 70 \text{ Hz}$
