questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A stretched string of length $1 \text{ m}$ and mass $40 \text{ g}$ is connected to a tuning fork. The tuning fork vibrates at $128 \text{ Hz}$ in a direction perpendicular to the string. Determine the tension required in the string for it to vibrate in four loops.
questions.solution:
Given:
Length of the string, $L = 1 \text{ m}$
Mass of the string, $m = 40 \text{ g} = 0.04 \text{ kg}$
Linear mass density, $\mu = \dfrac{m}{L} = 0.04 \text{ kg/m}$
Frequency of the tuning fork, $f = 128 \text{ Hz}$
Number of loops, $p = 4$

Since the tuning fork vibrates perpendicular to the string in Melde's experiment, the frequency of the string is equal to the frequency of the tuning fork.

The frequency of a stretched string vibrating in $p$ loops is given by:
$f = \dfrac{p}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

Substituting the given values:
$128 = \dfrac{4}{2 \times 1} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{0.04}}$

$128 = 2 \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{0.04}}$

$64 = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{0.04}}$

Squaring both sides:
$4096 = \dfrac{T}{0.04}$

$T = 4096 \times 0.04 = 163.84 \text{ N}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the required tension is $164 \text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wire fixed at both its ends is found to vibrate at resonant frequencies of $240 \text{ Hz}$ and $320 \text{ Hz}$. What could be the maximum value of the fundamental frequency?
questions.solution:
For a wire fixed at both ends, the resonant frequencies are given by $f_n = n f_0$, where $n$ is an integer and $f_0$ is the fundamental frequency.

The given resonant frequencies are $240 \text{ Hz}$ and $320 \text{ Hz}$.

Let $n_1 f_0 = 240$ and $n_2 f_0 = 320$ for some integers $n_1$ and $n_2$.

This implies that $f_0$ must be a common divisor of $240$ and $320$.

The maximum value of the fundamental frequency is the greatest common divisor (GCD) of $240$ and $320$.

$\text{GCD}(240, 320) = 80$

Thus, the maximum possible fundamental frequency is $80 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wire fixed at both its ends is found to vibrate at resonant frequencies of $240 \text{ Hz}$ and $320 \text{ Hz}$. If transverse waves travel on this string at a speed of $40 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, what is the length of the string?
questions.solution:
For a string fixed at both ends, the resonant frequencies are given by $f_n = \dfrac{nv}{2L}$, where $n$ is an integer representing the harmonic number, $v$ is the wave speed, and $L$ is the length of the string.

Assuming the given frequencies are consecutive resonant frequencies, their difference gives the fundamental frequency $f_1$:

$f_1 = f_{n+1} - f_n$

$f_1 = 320 \text{ Hz} - 240 \text{ Hz} = 80 \text{ Hz}$

The fundamental frequency is also given by the formula:

$f_1 = \dfrac{v}{2L}$

Substituting the given values ($f_1 = 80 \text{ Hz}$ and $v = 40 \text{ m s}^{-1}$):

$80 = \dfrac{40}{2L}$

$160L = 40$

$L = \dfrac{40}{160} \text{ m}$

$L = 0.25 \text{ m}$

Converting the length to centimeters:

$L = 0.25 \times 100 \text{ cm} = 25 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in a resonant mode, having a separation of $2.0 \text{ cm}$ between consecutive nodes. In the next higher resonant frequency, the separation decreases to $1.6 \text{ cm}$. Calculate the length of the string.
questions.solution:
Let the length of the string be $L$.

For a string fixed at both ends vibrating in the $n$-th harmonic, the separation between consecutive nodes is $\dfrac{\lambda}{2} = \dfrac{L}{n}$.

Given that for the $n$-th harmonic, the separation is $2.0 \text{ cm}$, we have:

$L = n \times 2.0$

For the next higher resonant mode, the string vibrates in the $(n+1)$-th harmonic. The separation between consecutive nodes becomes $1.6 \text{ cm}$, so:

$L = (n+1) \times 1.6$

Equating the two expressions for $L$:

$2.0 n = 1.6 (n+1)$

$2.0 n = 1.6 n + 1.6$

$0.4 n = 1.6$

$n = 4$

Substituting the value of $n$ into the first equation:

$L = 4 \times 2.0 = 8.0 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string clamped at both ends is set into vibration by a $660 \text{ Hz}$ tuning fork. The string vibrates in three loops, and the wave speed for a transverse wave on the string is $220 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Determine the length of the string.
questions.solution:
The wavelength $\lambda$ of the transverse wave is given by the ratio of wave speed to frequency:

$\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{220}{660} = \dfrac{1}{3} \text{ m}$

For a string clamped at both ends and vibrating in $n$ loops, the length $L$ of the string is related to the wavelength by:

$L = \dfrac{n \lambda}{2}$

Given that the string vibrates in $3$ loops, $n = 3$. Substituting the values:

$L = \dfrac{3 \times \dfrac{1}{3}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \text{ m}$

Converting the length to centimeters:

$L = 50 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string clamped at both ends is set into vibration by a $660 \text{ Hz}$ tuning fork, causing it to vibrate in three loops. The wave speed for a transverse wave on the string is $220 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. If the maximum amplitude of a particle is $0.5 \text{ cm}$, which of the following is a suitable equation describing the motion?
questions.solution:
Given frequency $f = 660 \text{ Hz}$ and wave speed $v = 220 \text{ m s}^{-1} = 22000 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$.

Angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 660 = 1320\pi \text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

Wave number $k = \dfrac{\omega}{v} = \dfrac{1320\pi}{22000} = 0.06\pi \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

Since the string is clamped at both ends, the displacement at $x = 0$ must be zero at all times. Therefore, the spatial part of the standing wave equation must be a sine function, $\sin(kx)$.

The maximum amplitude of the standing wave is given as $A = 0.5 \text{ cm}$.

The equation of the standing wave is of the form $y(x,t) = A \sin(kx) \cos(\omega t)$.

Substituting the values, we get:

$y(x,t) = (0.5 \text{ cm}) \sin[(0.06\pi \text{ cm}^{-1})x] \cos[(1320\pi \text{ s}^{-1})t]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A specific guitar wire has a length of $30.0 \text{ cm}$ and vibrates at a frequency of $196 \text{ Hz}$ when unobstructed. The subsequent higher notes on the scale are $220 \text{ Hz}$, $247 \text{ Hz}$, $262 \text{ Hz}$, and $294 \text{ Hz}$. At what distances from the end of the string must the finger be positioned to play these respective notes?
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is given by the formula:

$f = \dfrac{v}{2L}$

Since the tension and the linear mass density of the guitar wire remain constant, the wave speed $v$ is constant. Therefore, the fundamental frequency is inversely proportional to the vibrating length of the string:

$f \propto \dfrac{1}{L} \Rightarrow f_0 L_0 = f_1 L_1 = f_2 L_2 = \dots$

Given the original length $L_0 = 30.0 \text{ cm}$ and the original frequency $f_0 = 196 \text{ Hz}$, we can find the required vibrating lengths for the subsequent frequencies.

For $f_1 = 220 \text{ Hz}$:
$L_1 = \dfrac{f_0 L_0}{f_1} = \dfrac{196 \times 30.0}{220} = 26.72 \text{ cm} \approx 26.7 \text{ cm}$

For $f_2 = 247 \text{ Hz}$:
$L_2 = \dfrac{f_0 L_0}{f_2} = \dfrac{196 \times 30.0}{247} = 23.80 \text{ cm} \approx 23.8 \text{ cm}$

For $f_3 = 262 \text{ Hz}$:
$L_3 = \dfrac{f_0 L_0}{f_3} = \dfrac{196 \times 30.0}{262} = 22.44 \text{ cm} \approx 22.4 \text{ cm}$

For $f_4 = 294 \text{ Hz}$:
$L_4 = \dfrac{f_0 L_0}{f_4} = \dfrac{196 \times 30.0}{294} = 20.0 \text{ cm}$

These lengths represent the distances from the bridge (the lower end of the string) where the finger must be positioned to produce the respective notes. Thus, the required distances are $26.7 \text{ cm}$, $23.8 \text{ cm}$, $22.4 \text{ cm}$, and $20.0 \text{ cm}$.

Answer: $26.7 \text{ cm}$, $23.8 \text{ cm}$, $22.4 \text{ cm}$ and $20.0 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: Secured at both ends, a steel wire possesses a fundamental frequency of $200 \text{ Hz}$. A person is capable of hearing sound up to a maximum frequency of $14 \text{ kHz}$. Determine the highest harmonic that can be produced on this string and still remain audible to the person.
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of the string is given as $f_{1} = 200 \text{ Hz}$.

The maximum audible frequency for the person is $f_{\text{max}} = 14 \text{ kHz} = 14000 \text{ Hz}$.

The frequency of the $n^{\text{th}}$ harmonic of a string secured at both ends is given by $f_{n} = n f_{1}$.

For the sound to remain audible, the frequency of the harmonic must be less than or equal to the maximum audible frequency:

$f_{n} \le f_{\text{max}}$

$n \times 200 \le 14000$

$n \le \dfrac{14000}{200}$

$n \le 70$

The highest harmonic that can be produced and still remain audible is $70$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string has three resonant frequencies at $90 \text{ Hz}$, $150 \text{ Hz}$, and $210 \text{ Hz}$. Determine the highest possible fundamental frequency of vibration for this string.
questions.solution:
The resonant frequencies of a vibrating string are integer multiples of its fundamental frequency $f_0$.

Let the given resonant frequencies be $f_1 = 90 \text{ Hz}$, $f_2 = 150 \text{ Hz}$, and $f_3 = 210 \text{ Hz}$.

We have $f_1 = n_1 f_0$, $f_2 = n_2 f_0$, and $f_3 = n_3 f_0$, where $n_1, n_2, n_3$ are integers.

The highest possible fundamental frequency is the highest common factor (HCF) of the given resonant frequencies.

$f_0 = \text{HCF}(90, 150, 210)$

$90 = 30 \times 3$
$150 = 30 \times 5$
$210 = 30 \times 7$

The highest common factor is $30$.

Thus, the highest possible fundamental frequency is $30 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string exhibits three resonant frequencies at $90 \text{ Hz}$, $150 \text{ Hz}$, and $210 \text{ Hz}$. Identify which harmonics of the fundamental frequency these given frequencies correspond to.
questions.solution:
The given resonant frequencies are $90 \text{ Hz}$, $150 \text{ Hz}$, and $210 \text{ Hz}$.

The fundamental frequency $f_0$ is the highest common factor of the given resonant frequencies.

$f_0 = \text{HCF}(90, 150, 210) = 30 \text{ Hz}$

Expressing the given frequencies in terms of $f_0$:

$90 \text{ Hz} = 3 \times 30 \text{ Hz} = 3f_0$

$150 \text{ Hz} = 5 \times 30 \text{ Hz} = 5f_0$

$210 \text{ Hz} = 7 \times 30 \text{ Hz} = 7f_0$

Therefore, the given frequencies correspond to the 3rd, 5th, and 7th harmonics.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: Three resonant frequencies of a string are measured as $90 \text{ Hz}$, $150 \text{ Hz}$, and $210 \text{ Hz}$. Determine which overtones these given frequencies represent.
questions.solution:
The given resonant frequencies of the string are $90 \text{ Hz}$, $150 \text{ Hz}$, and $210 \text{ Hz}$.

The fundamental frequency $f_0$ is the highest common factor (HCF) of these frequencies.

$f_0 = \text{HCF}(90, 150, 210) = 30 \text{ Hz}$

The harmonic numbers corresponding to the given frequencies are:

$n_1 = \dfrac{90}{30} = 3$ (3rd harmonic)

$n_2 = \dfrac{150}{30} = 5$ (5th harmonic)

$n_3 = \dfrac{210}{30} = 7$ (7th harmonic)

For a string fixed at both ends, the $n^{\text{th}}$ harmonic corresponds to the $(n-1)^{\text{th}}$ overtone.

Therefore, the 3rd, 5th, and 7th harmonics correspond to the 2nd, 4th, and 6th overtones respectively.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: Three resonant frequencies of a string are observed to be $90 \text{ Hz}$, $150 \text{ Hz}$, and $210 \text{ Hz}$. If the string has a length of $80 \text{ cm}$, determine the speed of a transverse wave on this string.
questions.solution:
For a string fixed at both ends, the resonant frequencies are given by:

$f_n = n \dfrac{v}{2L}$

where $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ and $v$ is the speed of the transverse wave.

The given observed resonant frequencies are $90 \text{ Hz}$, $150 \text{ Hz}$, and $210 \text{ Hz}$. These frequencies must be integer multiples of the fundamental frequency $f_1$.

To find the fundamental frequency, we take the highest common factor (HCF) of the given frequencies:

$f_1 = \text{HCF}(90, 150, 210) = 30 \text{ Hz}$

The observed frequencies correspond to the 3rd, 5th, and 7th harmonics ($3f_1, 5f_1, 7f_1$), which are typically the modes excited when a string is plucked at its center (where even harmonics are absent).

Using the formula for the fundamental frequency:

$f_1 = \dfrac{v}{2L}$

Substituting the given values ($f_1 = 30 \text{ Hz}$ and $L = 80 \text{ cm} = 0.8 \text{ m}$):

$30 = \dfrac{v}{2 \times 0.8}$

$30 = \dfrac{v}{1.6}$

$v = 30 \times 1.6 = 48 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $48 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: Two wires are held tight between the same pair of supports. The tensions in the wires are in the ratio $2 : 1$, their radii are in the ratio $3 : 1$, and their densities are in the ratio $1 : 2$. Determine the ratio of their fundamental frequencies.
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of a stretched wire is given by:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

The linear mass density $\mu$ can be written in terms of the volume density $\rho$ and radius $r$ as $\mu = \pi r^2 \rho$. Substituting this in the frequency formula:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2Lr} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\pi \rho}}$

Since both wires are held between the same pair of supports, their lengths $L$ are equal. The ratio of their fundamental frequencies is:

$\dfrac{f_1}{f_2} = \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} \times \dfrac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}}$

Given $\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} = \dfrac{2}{1}$, $\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \dfrac{3}{1}$, and $\dfrac{\rho_1}{\rho_2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, we substitute these values:

$\dfrac{f_1}{f_2} = \dfrac{1}{3} \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{1} \times \dfrac{2}{1}}$

$\dfrac{f_1}{f_2} = \dfrac{1}{3} \sqrt{4} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: As shown in the figure, a uniform horizontal rod of length $40 \text{ cm}$ and mass $1.2 \text{ kg}$ is supported by two identical wires. Where must a mass of $4.8 \text{ kg}$ be positioned on the rod such that the same tuning fork can excite the left wire into its fundamental vibrations and the right wire into its first overtone? Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
Let $T_L$ and $T_R$ be the tensions in the left and right wires respectively.

The frequency of the fundamental mode of the left wire is $f_L = \dfrac{1}{2l} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_L}{\mu}}$.

The frequency of the first overtone of the right wire is $f_R = \dfrac{2}{2l} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_R}{\mu}}$.

Since both wires are excited by the same tuning fork, their frequencies are equal:

$\dfrac{1}{2l} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_L}{\mu}} = \dfrac{2}{2l} \sqrt{\dfrac{T_R}{\mu}}$

$\Rightarrow \sqrt{T_L} = 2\sqrt{T_R} \Rightarrow T_L = 4T_R$

For translational equilibrium of the rod, the total upward force equals the total downward force:

$T_L + T_R = mg + Mg$

$4T_R + T_R = 1.2g + 4.8g$

$5T_R = 6.0g \Rightarrow T_R = 1.2g$

Then, $T_L = 4.8g$.

Let the mass of $4.8 \text{ kg}$ be placed at a distance $x$ from the left end. For rotational equilibrium, taking torque about the left end:

$T_R \times 40 - mg \times 20 - Mg \times x = 0$

$1.2g \times 40 - 1.2g \times 20 - 4.8g \times x = 0$

$48 - 24 - 4.8x = 0$

$4.8x = 24 \Rightarrow x = 5 \text{ cm}$

Thus, the mass must be positioned $5 \text{ cm}$ from the left end.

questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: As shown in the figure, an aluminium wire of length $60 \text{ cm}$ is connected to a steel wire of length $80 \text{ cm}$, and the combination is stretched between two fixed supports, producing a tension of $40 \text{ N}$. The steel wire has a cross-sectional area of $1.0 \text{ mm}^2$, while the aluminium wire has a cross-sectional area of $3.0 \text{ mm}^2$. Determine the minimum frequency of a tuning fork that can set up standing waves in the system such that the joint acts as a node. (Given: the density of aluminium is $2.6 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$ and that of steel is $7.8 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$).
questions.solution:
The linear mass density of the steel wire is given by:

$\mu_s = \rho_s A_s = (7.8 \times 10^3 \text{ kg m}^{-3})(1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2) = 7.8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg m}^{-1}$

The linear mass density of the aluminium wire is:

$\mu_a = \rho_a A_a = (2.6 \times 10^3 \text{ kg m}^{-3})(3.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2) = 7.8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg m}^{-1}$

Since $\mu_s = \mu_a = \mu$, the wave speed $v$ is the same in both wires:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{40}{7.8 \times 10^{-3}}} \approx 71.6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

For the joint to act as a node, both wires must form standing waves with nodes at their ends. The frequency $f$ must be the same for both wires:

$f = \dfrac{n_s v}{2L_s} = \dfrac{n_a v}{2L_a}$

where $n_s$ and $n_a$ are the number of loops in the steel and aluminium wires, respectively. Equating the two expressions gives:

$\dfrac{n_s}{L_s} = \dfrac{n_a}{L_a} \Rightarrow \dfrac{n_s}{0.8} = \dfrac{n_a}{0.6} \Rightarrow \dfrac{n_s}{n_a} = \dfrac{4}{3}$

For the minimum frequency, $n_s$ and $n_a$ must be the smallest possible integers. Thus, $n_s = 4$ and $n_a = 3$.

Substituting $n_s = 4$ into the frequency formula yields:

$f = \dfrac{4 \times 71.6}{2 \times 0.8} = \dfrac{71.6}{0.4} = 179 \text{ Hz}$

The closest value among the given options is $180 \text{ Hz}$.

Answer: $180 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q:
A string of length $L$ secured at both ends vibrates in its fundamental mode with a frequency $
u$ and a maximum amplitude $A$. Determine the wavelength and the wave number $k$.
questions.solution:
For a string of length $L$ secured at both ends, the fundamental mode of vibration consists of a single loop.

The distance between two consecutive nodes is $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$.

Since the string is fixed at both ends, the length of the string is equal to half the wavelength.

$L = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$

$\lambda = 2L$

The wave number $k$ is defined as:

$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$

Substituting $\lambda = 2L$:

$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{2L} = \dfrac{\pi}{L}$

Thus, the wavelength is $2L$ and the wave number is $\dfrac{\pi}{L}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string of length $L$ secured at both ends vibrates in its fundamental mode with a frequency $\nu$ and a maximum amplitude $A$. Choose the origin at one end of the string and the $X$-axis along the string. Let the $Y$-axis be along the direction of displacement. Set $t = 0$ at the instant the middle point of the string crosses its mean position travelling towards the positive $y$-direction. Determine the equation describing the standing wave.
questions.solution:
The general equation of a standing wave is $y(x, t) = f(x) g(t)$.

Since the string is fixed at $x = 0$ and $x = L$, the displacement at these points must be zero. This requires the spatial part to be a sine function: $f(x) = A \sin(kx)$.

For the fundamental mode, the string vibrates in a single loop, which means $L = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \Rightarrow \lambda = 2L$.

The wave number is $k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2\pi}{2L} = \dfrac{\pi}{L}$.

Thus, the spatial part is $f(x) = A \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{L}\right)$.

The temporal part is given by $g(t) = \sin(\omega t + \phi)$.

At $t = 0$, the middle point of the string ($x = \dfrac{L}{2}$) crosses the mean position ($y = 0$), which gives $g(0) = 0$. This implies $\phi = 0$ or $\pi$.

Since the particle is travelling towards the positive $y$-direction, the velocity $\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}$ at $t = 0$ must be positive.

The velocity is proportional to $\omega \cos(\omega t + \phi)$. For this to be positive at $t = 0$, we must have $\phi = 0$.

Therefore, the temporal part is $g(t) = \sin(\omega t) = \sin(2\pi \nu t)$.

Combining the spatial and temporal parts, the equation of the standing wave is $y = A \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{L}\right) \sin(2\pi \nu t)$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string, $2 \text{ m}$ long and fixed at both ends, is set into vibrations in its first overtone. The wave speed on the string is $200 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the amplitude is $0.5 \text{ cm}$. Determine the wavelength and the frequency.
questions.solution:
For a string of length $L$ fixed at both ends, the wavelength of the $n$-th harmonic is given by $\lambda = \dfrac{2L}{n}$.

The first overtone corresponds to the second harmonic, so $n = 2$.

Substituting $L = 2 \text{ m}$ and $n = 2$:

$\lambda = \dfrac{2 \times 2}{2} = 2 \text{ m}$

The frequency of the wave is given by $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda}$.

Given the wave speed $v = 200 \text{ m s}^{-1}$:

$f = \dfrac{200}{2} = 100 \text{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A string, $2 \text{ m}$ long and fixed at both ends, is set into vibrations in its first overtone. The wave speed on the string is $200 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the amplitude is $0.5 \text{ cm}$. Determine the equation giving the displacement of different points as a function of time. Choose the $X$-axis along the string with the origin at one end and $t = 0$ at the instant when the point $x = 50 \text{ cm}$ has reached its maximum displacement.
questions.solution:
For a string fixed at both ends, the wavelength in the first overtone ($n = 2$) is given by $L = 2 \left(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\right) = \lambda$.

Given $L = 2 \text{ m}$, we have $\lambda = 2 \text{ m}$.

The wave number $k$ is $k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} = \pi \text{ m}^{-1}$.

The angular frequency $\omega$ is $\omega = v k = 200 \times \pi = 200\pi \text{ s}^{-1}$.

The general equation for a standing wave with nodes at $x = 0$ and $x = L$ is $y(x, t) = A \sin(kx) \cos(\omega t + \phi)$.

Given the amplitude $A = 0.5 \text{ cm}$.

At $t = 0$, the point $x = 50 \text{ cm} = 0.5 \text{ m}$ has maximum displacement.

Substituting $x = 0.5 \text{ m}$ into the spatial part gives $\sin(\pi \times 0.5) = 1$, which means it is an antinode.

For the displacement to be maximum at $t = 0$, the temporal part $\cos(\omega \times 0 + \phi) = \cos(\phi)$ must be $1$, giving $\phi = 0$.

Therefore, the equation of the standing wave is $y(x, t) = (0.5 \text{ cm}) \sin[(\pi \text{ m}^{-1})x] \cos[(200\pi \text{ s}^{-1})t]$.

questions.q: A string fixed at both ends is vibrating in its third harmonic. The equation for its vibration is given by $y = (0.4 \text{ cm}) \sin[(0.314 \text{ cm}^{-1}) x] \cos[(600\pi \text{ s}^{-1})t]$. Determine the frequency of vibration.
questions.solution:
The standard equation of a standing wave is given by $y = A \sin(kx) \cos(\omega t)$.

Comparing the given equation $y = (0.4 \text{ cm}) \sin[(0.314 \text{ cm}^{-1}) x] \cos[(600\pi \text{ s}^{-1})t]$ with the standard equation, we get the angular frequency $\omega = 600\pi \text{ rad/s}$.

The frequency of vibration is given by $f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$.

Substituting the value of $\omega$, we get $f = \dfrac{600\pi}{2\pi} = 300 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.q: A string fixed at both ends is vibrating in its third harmonic. The equation for its vibration is given by $y = (0.4 \text{ cm}) \sin[(0.314 \text{ cm}^{-1}) x] \cos[(600\pi \text{ s}^{-1})t]$. Determine the positions of the nodes.
questions.solution:
The equation of the standing wave is given by $y = 0.4 \sin(0.314 x) \cos(600\pi t)$.

The amplitude of the wave at position $x$ is $A = 0.4 \sin(0.314 x)$.

For nodes, the amplitude must be zero, which gives:

$\sin(0.314 x) = 0$

$0.314 x = n\pi$, where $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$

Using $\pi = 3.14$, we get:

$0.314 x = n(3.14)$

$x = 10n \text{ cm}$

The positions of the nodes are $x = 0, 10, 20, 30, \dots \text{ cm}$.

The wave number is $k = 0.314 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, so the wavelength is $\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = \dfrac{2 \times 3.14}{0.314} = 20 \text{ cm}$.

Since the string is vibrating in its third harmonic, the length of the string is $L = 3 \left(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\right) = 3 \times \dfrac{20}{2} = 30 \text{ cm}$.

Thus, the nodes on the string are located at $x = 0, 10 \text{ cm}, 20 \text{ cm}, 30 \text{ cm}$.

$k = 0.314 \text{ cm}^{-1}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$, we have:

$\lambda = \dfrac{6.28}{0.314} = 20 \text{ cm}$

For a string fixed at both ends vibrating in its third harmonic, the length of the string $L$ is given by:

$L = \dfrac{3\lambda}{2}$

Substituting the value of $\lambda$:

$L = \dfrac{3 \times 20}{2} = 30 \text{ cm}$

The equation for its vibration is given by $y = (0.4 \text{ cm}) \sin[(0.314 \text{ cm}^{-1}) x] \cos[(600\pi \text{ s}^{-1})t]$. Determine the wavelength and the speed of the two travelling waves that can interfere to produce this vibration.

The given equation of the standing wave is $y = 0.4 \sin(0.314 x) \cos(600\pi t)$.

Comparing this with the standard equation of a standing wave $y = 2A \sin(kx) \cos(\omega t)$, we get:

$k = 0.314 \text{ cm}^{-1}$

$\omega = 600\pi \text{ s}^{-1}$

The wavelength $\lambda$ is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = \dfrac{2 \times 3.14}{0.314} = 20 \text{ cm}$

The speed $v$ of the travelling waves is given by:

$v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} = \dfrac{600\pi}{0.314} = \dfrac{600 \times 3.14}{0.314} = 6000 \text{ cm/s} = 60 \text{ m/s}$

The equation of the standing wave is given by $y = A \sin(kx) \cos(\omega t)$.

Comparing the given equation with the standard form, we get $k = 0.314 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

We know that $k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$.

$\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} = 0.314 \Rightarrow \dfrac{2 \times 3.14}{\lambda} = 0.314 \Rightarrow \lambda = 20 \text{ cm}$.

For a string fixed at both ends, the length of the string must be an integral multiple of $\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$.

$L = n\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ where $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$

For the smallest possible length, $n = 1$.

$L_{min} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = \dfrac{20}{2} = 10 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A wire of length $40 \text{ cm}$ and mass $3.2 \text{ g}$ is stretched between two fixed supports located $40.05 \text{ cm}$ apart. The wire vibrates at $220 \text{ Hz}$ in its fundamental mode. Determine the Young modulus of the wire, given that its cross-sectional area is $1.0 \text{ mm}^2$.
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is given by:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

where $L$ is the vibrating length and $\mu$ is the linear mass density. Since $\mu = \dfrac{m}{L}$, we have:

$f = \dfrac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T L}{m}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{mL}}$

Squaring both sides, the tension $T$ in the wire is:

$T = 4 f^2 mL$

Approximating $L \approx L_0 = 0.4 \text{ m}$ for the tension calculation:

$T = 4 \times (220)^2 \times (3.2 \times 10^{-3}) \times 0.4 = 247.8 \text{ N}$

The Young's modulus $Y$ is given by:

$Y = \dfrac{T L_0}{A \Delta L}$

where $L_0 = 0.4 \text{ m}$, $A = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$, and $\Delta L = 40.05 - 40 = 0.05 \text{ cm} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$.

$Y = \dfrac{247.8 \times 0.4}{1.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 5 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{99.12}{5 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.98 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$

Answer: $1.98 \times 10^{11} \text{ N/m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: As depicted in the figure, a string is stretched by a block going over a pulley. The string vibrates in its tenth harmonic in unison with a specific tuning fork. When a beaker containing water is positioned under the block such that the block becomes completely submerged, the string vibrates in its eleventh harmonic. Determine the density of the material of the block.
questions.solution:
The frequency of the $n$-th harmonic of a stretched string is given by:

$f = \dfrac{n}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

where $T$ is the tension in the string, $L$ is its length, and $\mu$ is its linear mass density.

Initially, the block is in the air, and the tension $T_1$ is equal to the weight of the block:

$T_1 = V \rho g$

where $V$ is the volume of the block and $\rho$ is its density. The string vibrates in its 10th harmonic, so the frequency is:

$f = \dfrac{10}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{V \rho g}{\mu}}$

When the block is completely submerged in water, the tension $T_2$ is reduced due to the buoyant force:

$T_2 = V \rho g - V \rho_w g = V (\rho - \rho_w) g$

where $\rho_w = 10^3 \text{ kg/m}^3$ is the density of water. The string now vibrates in its 11th harmonic with the same frequency:

$f = \dfrac{11}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{V (\rho - \rho_w) g}{\mu}}$

Equating the two expressions for frequency:

$\dfrac{10}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{V \rho g}{\mu}} = \dfrac{11}{2L} \sqrt{\dfrac{V (\rho - \rho_w) g}{\mu}}$

Squaring both sides, we get:

$100 \rho = 121 (\rho - \rho_w)$

Solving for $\rho$:

$121 \rho_w = 121 \rho - 100 \rho$

$21 \rho = 121 \rho_w$

$\rho = \dfrac{121}{21} \rho_w$

Substituting $\rho_w = 10^3 \text{ kg/m}^3$:

$\rho = \dfrac{121}{21} \times 10^3 \text{ kg/m}^3 \approx 5.76 \times 10^3 \text{ kg/m}^3$

Rounding to one decimal place, the density of the material of the block is $5.8 \times 10^3 \text{ kg/m}^3$.

questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A rope of length $2.00 \text{ m}$ and mass $80 \text{ g}$ is fixed at one end and tied to a light string at the other end. The tension in the string is $256 \text{ N}$. Determine the frequencies of the fundamental and the first two overtones.
questions.solution:
The linear mass density of the rope is given by:

$\mu = \dfrac{m}{L} = \dfrac{80 \times 10^{-3}}{2.00} = 0.04 \text{ kg/m}$

The speed of the transverse wave on the rope is:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{256}{0.04}} = \sqrt{6400} = 80 \text{ m/s}$

The rope is fixed at one end, which acts as a node. The other end is tied to a light string (negligible mass), which provides no inertia and thus acts as a free end (antinode). The system behaves like a string fixed at one end and free at the other.

The allowed frequencies (harmonics) for such a system are odd multiples of the fundamental frequency, given by:

$f_n = \dfrac{(2n-1)v}{4L}$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$

The fundamental frequency ($n=1$) is:

$f_1 = \dfrac{v}{4L} = \dfrac{80}{4 \times 2.00} = 10 \text{ Hz}$

The first overtone corresponds to the third harmonic ($n=2$):

$f_2 = 3f_1 = 3 \times 10 = 30 \text{ Hz}$

The second overtone corresponds to the fifth harmonic ($n=3$):

$f_3 = 5f_1 = 5 \times 10 = 50 \text{ Hz}$

Thus, the frequencies are $10 \text{ Hz}$, $30 \text{ Hz}$, and $50 \text{ Hz}$.

questions.q: A rope of length $2.00 \text{ m}$ and mass $80 \text{ g}$ is fixed at one end and tied to a light string at the other end. The tension in the string is $256 \text{ N}$. Determine the wavelengths corresponding to the fundamental and the first two overtones.
questions.solution:
The rope is fixed at one end and tied to a light string at the other end. The fixed end acts as a node and the end tied to the light string acts as a free end (antinode).

For a string fixed at one end and free at the other, the length $L$ is related to the wavelength $\lambda$ by:

$L = (2n + 1)\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$

The allowed wavelengths are given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{4L}{2n + 1}$

Given $L = 2.00 \text{ m}$.

For the fundamental mode ($n = 0$):

$\lambda_0 = \dfrac{4 \times 2.00}{1} = 8.00 \text{ m}$

For the first overtone ($n = 1$):

$\lambda_1 = \dfrac{4 \times 2.00}{3} = \dfrac{8.00}{3} \approx 2.67 \text{ m}$

For the second overtone ($n = 2$):

$\lambda_2 = \dfrac{4 \times 2.00}{5} = \dfrac{8.00}{5} = 1.60 \text{ m}$

questions.chapter: Wave Motion and Waves on a String
questions.q: A heavy string is fastened at one end to a movable support and at the other end to a light thread, as shown in the figure. The light thread passes over a fixed pulley, suspending a weight that creates tension. The lowest resonant frequency of the heavy string is $120 \text{ Hz}$. The movable support is then pushed $10 \text{ cm}$ to the right, causing the joint to rest on the pulley. Determine the new minimum frequency at which the heavy string can resonate.
questions.solution:
Initially, the heavy string is fixed at the movable support and attached to a light thread at the other end. Since the light thread has negligible mass, it cannot support a transverse force. Therefore, the joint acts as a free end (an antinode) for the transverse waves in the heavy string.

For a string of length $L$ fixed at one end and free at the other, the lowest resonant (fundamental) frequency is given by:
$f_1 = \dfrac{v}{4L} = 120 \text{ Hz}$

When the movable support is pushed $10 \text{ cm}$ to the right, the entire heavy string shifts by $10 \text{ cm}$, causing the joint to rest exactly on the fixed pulley. The pulley restricts any transverse motion, so this end now acts as a fixed end (a node).

The heavy string is now fixed at both ends. Its length $L$ remains unchanged, and the tension $T$ (provided by the suspended weight) and mass per unit length $\mu$ also remain constant. Thus, the wave speed $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$ is unchanged.

For a string fixed at both ends, the new lowest resonant frequency is:
$f_1' = \dfrac{v}{2L}$

Comparing the two frequencies, we get:
$f_1' = 2 \times \left(\dfrac{v}{4L}\right) = 2 \times f_1$

Substituting the given value:
$f_1' = 2 \times 120 \text{ Hz} = 240 \text{ Hz}$

Answer: $240 \text{ Hz}$
